claim: A 6-week subchronic ototoxic protocol induces transient and partial vestibular loss which equally affects the canal- and otolith-dependent VORs.
source: Here, we first demonstrate the efficacy of a 6-week subchronic ototoxic protocol in inducing transient and partial vestibular loss which equally affects the canal- and otolith-dependent VORs.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2 showing VOR and OCR measurements over time.

claim: Organ-specific alteration of type I, but not type II, hair cells correlates with functional impairments in vestibular reflexes.
source: Immunostaining of hair cells in the vestibular sensory epithelia revealed that organ-specific alteration of type I, but not type II, hair cells correlates with functional impairments.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3, demonstrating correlations between type I HC markers and VOR/OCR function.

claim: The decrease in VOR performance is paralleled with an increase in the gain of the OKR occurring in a specific range of frequencies where VOR normally dominates gaze stabilization.
source: The decrease in VOR performance is paralleled with an increase in the gain of the OKR occurring in a specific range of frequencies where VOR normally dominates gaze stabilization, compatible with a sensory substitution process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5 showing frequency-specific OKR increases corresponding to VOR decreases.

claim: Visuo-vestibular interactions remain reduced despite a significant recovery in the VOR.
source: Comparison of unimodal OKR or VOR versus bimodal CGR revealed that visuo-vestibular interactions remain reduced despite a significant recovery in the VOR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CGR data and modeling results presented in Figure 6.

claim: The differential capacity to optimally combine OKR and VOR correlates with the reproducibility of the VOR responses.
source: Modeling and sweep-based analysis revealed that the differential capacity to optimally combine OKR and VOR correlates with the reproducibility of the VOR responses.
evidence: This is supported by the sweep-based analysis and correlation data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: The vestibular system participates in essential functions such as balance, postural control and gaze stabilization together with the optokinetic system.
source: The vestibular system is well-preserved amongst vertebrates, participating in essential functions such as balance, postural control and, together with the optokinetic system, gaze stabilization (Straka et al., 2016; Wibble et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature (Straka et al., 2016; Wibble et al., 2022).

claim: Vestibular signals contribute to cognitive processes such as spatial orientation and navigation.
source: Beyond these recognized roles, vestibular signals also contribute to cognitive processes for example spatial orientation and navigation (Cullen, 2019), or body representation (Lopez et al., 2012; Facchini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research (Cullen, 2019; Lopez et al., 2012; Facchini et al., 2021).

claim: Vestibular pathologies affecting the inner ear are associated with significant deterioration of patient well-being.
source: Because of its involvement in many basic functions important in our daily life, vestibular pathologies affecting the inner ear are associated with a significant deterioration of the well-being of patients (Möhwald et al., 2020) and represent an important public health concern (Agrawal et al., 2009; Agrawal et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies (Möhwald et al., 2020; Agrawal et al., 2009; Agrawal et al., 2013).

claim: Vestibular compensation involves dynamical multisensory reweighting of proprioceptive and visual inputs and internal efferent copies.
source: The compensation taking place after the lesion is known to involve dynamical multisensory reweighting of proprioceptive and visual inputs and of internal efferent copies (Cullen et al., 2010; Sadeghi et al., 2012; Sadeghi and Beraneck, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on vestibular compensation mechanisms (Cullen et al., 2010; Sadeghi et al., 2012; Sadeghi and Beraneck, 2020).

claim: Clinical situations of vestibular function loss are often only partial and/or transient rather than total and permanent.
source: While total and permanent lesions offer the experimental opportunity to characterize drastic cellular and molecular changes triggered by the total silencing of the vestibular endorgans, they imperfectly mimic clinical situations where peripheral vestibular function loss is only partial and/or transient (Bisdorff et al., 2009; Lopez-Escamez et al., 2015; Brandt and Dieterich, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature (Bisdorff et al., 2009; Lopez-Escamez et al., 2015; Brandt and Dieterich, 2017).

claim: Subchronic exposure to IDPN in drinking water at low doses allows for progressive ototoxicity leading to partial and largely reversible loss of function.
source: Subchronic exposure to IDPN in drinking water at low doses allowed for progressive ototoxicity, leading to a partial and largely reversible loss of function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Sedó-Cabezón et al., 2015; Martins-Lopes et al., 2019; Greguske et al., 2019) and by the experimental data in the current study.

claim: The subchronic IDPN protocol causes postural and locomotor deficits.
source: Although the subchronic IDPN protocol was shown to cause postural and locomotor deficits (Martins-Lopes et al., 2019), its effects on the gaze stabilizing reflexes, namely the vestibulo-ocular and optokinetic reflexes, have not yet been described.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martins-Lopes et al., 2019.

claim: Quantification of the vestibulo-ocular reflexes is a sensitive and specific method to assess the functionality of the sensory-motor vestibular pathway.
source: Quantification of the vestibulo-ocular reflexes is a sensitive and specific method to assess the functionality of the sensory-motor vestibular pathway; it is the most used test in clinics, and highly correlates to quality-of-life reports in patients suffering from acute peripheral diseases (Möhwald et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature (Möhwald et al., 2020) and established clinical knowledge.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the vestibular pathway demonstrates recruitment of circuits involved in visual processing at midbrain, thalamic and cortical regions.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of the vestibular pathway demonstrated the recruitment of circuits involved in visual processing at the midbrain, thalamic and cortical regions (Leong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leong et al., 2019.

claim: Acute vestibular loss triggers brain-wide adaptive plasticity in circuits involved in visual processing.
source: Recent imaging studies in rodents have shown that acute vestibular loss triggers brain-wide adaptive plasticity in circuits known to be involved in visual processing (Zwergal et al., 2016; Grosch et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to imaging studies (Zwergal et al., 2016; Grosch et al., 2021).

claim: OKR plasticity is triggered during vestibular compensation following permanent vestibular lesion.
source: In addition, it was previously shown that OKR plasticity is triggered during vestibular compensation following a permanent vestibular lesion (Faulstich et al., 2006; Nelson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Faulstich et al., 2006; Nelson et al., 2017).

claim: The aVOR gain of the IDPN group significantly decreased starting at week 4 compared to week 0.
source: However, starting W4 the aVOR gain of IDPN group significantly decreased with respect to W0 (Newman-Keuls post hoc test: IDPN W0 vs W4 p<10–4, see Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: The aVOR gain of the IDPN group was significantly lower compared with the SHAM group at week 4.
source: and was significantly lower compared with the SHAM group (W4, IDPN vs SHAM p<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The minimum aVOR gain in IDPN-treated mice was reached at week 6, corresponding to approximately 2/3 of aVOR loss.
source: with a minimum reached at W6 corresponding to ~2/3 of aVOR loss (IDPN W4 vs W6 p<10–4, IDPN W6 vs W8 p=0.043762).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the end of 6 weeks of washout, the mean aVOR significantly improved to levels observed at week 4.
source: At the end of the 6 weeks of washout, the mean aVOR significantly improved (IDPN W6 vs W12 p<10–4) to levels observed at W4 (IDPN W4 vs W12 p=0.561969).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The amplitude and dynamic of aVOR gain changes were similar for all frequencies >0.2 Hz.
source: Notably, the amplitude and dynamic of gain changes were similar for all frequencies >0.2 Hz (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At the lowest frequency tested (0.2 Hz), aVOR gain decrease reached significance only at week 6.
source: However, at the lowest frequency tested (0.2 Hz), aVOR gain decrease reached significance only at W6.
evidence: This is supported by frequency-specific analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: aVOR responses were modified by significant phase leads that affected all frequencies starting week 6.
source: aVOR responses were further modified by significant phase leads that affected all frequencies starting W6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, ANOVA repeated measures Weeks x Group Interactions F(6, 246)=14.528, p<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was a significant difference in OCR gain between SHAM and IDPN during initial measurements at week 0.
source: We note that there was a significant difference between SHAM and IDPN during the initial measurements at W0, before any treatment.
evidence: This is noted in the text and visible in Figure 1F.

claim: The incidental difference in OCR gain between groups at week 0 completely disappeared at week 2.
source: However, at this timepoint mice were not yet separated into different groups. This incidental difference completely disappeared on the measurement performed at W2 (W2 IDPN vs SHAM p=0.8135).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The OCR responses of the IDPN group significantly decreased at week 4 compared to the SHAM group.
source: While the gain of the SHAM group stays in a 0.5–0.6 range over the whole duration of the protocol, the responses of the IDPN group significantly decreased at W4 compared to the SHAM group (W4 IDPN vs SHAM p<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The OCR decrease in IDPN-treated mice was larger at week 6 compared to week 4.
source: This decrease was larger at W6 (IDPN W4 vs W6 p=0.023)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At weeks 10 and 12, the OCR of IDPN group recovered to a level comparable to the SHAM group.
source: At W10 and W12, the OCR of IDPN group recovered to a level comparable to the SHAM group (W10 IDPN vs SHAM p=0.1262, W12 IPDN vs SHAM p=0.3385).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The maculo-ocular reflex (MOR) bias decreased significantly compared to the SHAM group starting week 2 of treatment.
source: The maculo-ocular reflex (MOR) bias decreased significantly compared to the SHAM group (ANOVA Weeks x Group, F(6, 132)=10.076, p<10–4) starting W2 of treatment (W2 IDPN vs SHAM p=0.0018), demonstrating that ototoxicity already affected the vestibular system at this early time point.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of OVAR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The maximal decrease in MOR bias was reached at week 6.
source: The maximal decrease was reached at W6 (W6 IDPN vs SHAM p=0.00012)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of OVAR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MOR bias recovery led to normal responses at week 12.
source: and recovery led to normal responses at W12 (W12 IDPN vs SHAM p=0.4709).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of OVAR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Alteration in canal- and otolith-dependent responses followed a very similar time course.
source: Alteration in canal- and otolith-dependent responses followed a very similar time course (OCR vs aVOR at 1 HZ on Figure 2A; similar patterns were obtained with the other tested frequencies (not shown)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of aVOR and OCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At week 6, there was a significant correlation between the amplitude of changes observed in aVOR and OCR.
source: At W6, there was a significant correlation between the amplitude of the changes observed in aVOR and OCR, such that canalar and otolithic loss of function was proportional (slope of regression line: 0.5586).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The significant correlation between aVOR and OCR changes was preserved at week 12.
source: Despite the general recovery, this significant correlation was preserved at W12: the recovery in canal-dependent responses was proportional to the recovery in otolith-dependent responses (slope of regression line: 0.5566).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Six-week long treatment of IDPN exposure led to a significant reduction in the labelling of type I HC in the canal crista.
source: Six-week long treatment of IDPN exposure led to a significant reduction in the labelling of type I HC in the canal crista (quantified in Figure 3A2, Non parametric Kruskal-Wallis test, SHAM vs IDPN Spp1, p=0.0322; SHAM vs IDPN CASPR1, p=0.0268; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A1 and B1 for the peripheral zones)
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A2.

claim: IDPN treatment led to a significant reduction in type I HC labelling in the otolith macula.
source: and in the otolith macula (Figure 3C2, Non parametric Kruskal Wallis test SHAM vs IDPN Spp1, p=0.0279; SHAM vs IDPN CASPR1, p=0.0343).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C2.

claim: IDPN treatment did not alter type II HC-specific labelling in vestibular endorgans.
source: However, the treatment did not alter type II HC-specific labelling as the number of Calre + cells in the IDPN group was similar to the SHAM in all regions of either vestibular endorgans (Figure 3A2, canal crista, Calre: Non parametric Kruskal-Wallis test IDPN vs SHAM, p>0.9999; Figure 3C2, otolith macula, Calre: SHAM vs IDPN, P>0.9999).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 3A2 and 3C2.

claim: The total number of HC marked with Myo7a was not significantly different between IDPN-treated mice and SHAM.
source: Importantly, the total number of HC marked with Myo7a (labelling both type I and type II HC) was not significantly different between the IDPN-treated mice and the SHAM, suggesting that the alteration of type I HC is not associated with cell loss.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 3A2 and 3C2.

claim: At week 12, the number of type I HC labelled in IDPN-treated mice was no longer significantly different from the SHAM group in either endorgan.
source: Moreover, at W12 the number of type I HC labelled in the IDPN-treated mice was no longer significantly different from the SHAM group in either endorgans (Figure 3A3 for crista; Figure 3C3 for macula).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 3A3 and 3C3.

claim: Both markers of type I HC (CASPR1 and Spp1) were significantly correlated with the aVOR gain.
source: Both markers of type I HC (CASPR1 and Spp1, left panels) were significantly correlated with the aVOR gain (linear regression, Spp1: r2=0.5128, p=0.0001; CASPR1: r2=0.4948, p=0.0002)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B1.

claim: The number of type II HC in the ampulla did not correlate with variation observed in aVOR function.
source: whereas the rather constant number of type II HC in the ampulla did not correlate with the variation observed in aVOR function.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B1.

claim: The numbers of type I HC in the striolar region of the utricule correlated with OCR gain.
source: The numbers of type I HC and II HC found in the striolar region of the utricule are similarly plotted in relation to the OCR gain (linear regression, Spp1: r2=0.6011, p<0.0001; CASPR1: r2=0.6342, p<0.0001, Figure 3D1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D1.

claim: The otolithic function correlated with the number of type I HC, and not type II HC in the central region.
source: Again, the otolithic function correlated with the number of type I HC, and not type II HC in the central region.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D1.

claim: The ototoxic effect of IDPN induces a transient biochemical alteration of type I HC rather than definitive hair cell degeneration.
source: Taken together, comparison at W6 and W12 of non-specific HC and type I-specific HC markers suggest that the ototoxic effect induces a transient biochemical alteration of type I HC rather than a definitive hair cell degeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the recovery of type I HC markers at W12 and the lack of significant Myo7a cell loss, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: IDPN-induced alteration of canal and otolith functions are correlated with the ototoxic effect on type I, and not type II, HC.
source: Overall, IDPN-induced alteration of canal and otolith functions are correlated with the ototoxic effect on type I, and not type II, HC in the central and peripheral zones of vestibular endorgans.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean OKR gain of IDPN mice was significantly different from the mean OKR gain of SHAM mice at week 8.
source: The mean OKR gain of IDPN mice was significantly different from the mean OKR gain of SHAM mice at W8 (interaction between Weeks and Group F(6,132)=2.9845, p=0.0091; IDPN W0 vs W8, p=0.0216, see Table 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) where it reached its peak (IDPN W0 vs W8, p=0.00037).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of OKR data shown in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claim: The OKR gain stayed significantly larger compared to SHAM through the end of the washout period at week 12.
source: The gain stayed significantly larger compared to the SHAM through the end of the washout period (W12 IDPN vs SHAM, p=0.046).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of OKR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At week 6, there was a significant difference between the gain of IDPN and SHAM groups limited to frequencies 0.5 and 1 Hz.
source: At W6, there was a significant difference between the gain of the IDPN and SHAM groups limited to the frequencies 0.5 and 1 Hz (W6 IDPN vs. SHAM, 0.5 Hz, p=0.013117; W6 IDPN vs. SHAM, 1 Hz, p<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by frequency-specific analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At week 8, OKR gains measured at frequencies above 0.2 Hz were significantly increased compared to the SHAM group.
source: At W8, the gains measured at frequencies above 0.2 Hz were significantly increased compared to the SHAM group (W8 IDPN vs. SHAM, 0.33 Hz, p=0.027687; 0.5 Hz, p=0.0025; 1 Hz, p=0.00015).
evidence: This is supported by frequency-specific analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: OKR responses at higher frequencies (0.33, 0.5, and 1 Hz) were significantly increased.
source: Globally, responses at higher frequencies (0.33, 0.5, and 1 Hz) were significantly increased (ANOVA Weeks x Group x Frequencies interaction, F(24, 528)=6.5870, p<10–4)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of frequency-specific OKR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: OKR responses at the lowest frequencies (0.1 and 0.2 Hz) were not significantly modulated.
source: whereas responses at the lowest frequencies (0.1 and 0.2 Hz) were not significantly modulated.
evidence: This is supported by frequency-specific analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Changes in OKR gain for frequencies >0.2 Hz were not accompanied by changes in the timing (phase) of the OKR.
source: Additionally, these changes in gain for frequencies >0.2 Hz were not accompanied by changes in the timing (phase) of the OKR (Figure 4E; ANOVA, Weeks x Group x Frequencies interaction, p=0.3802).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of phase data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The vast majority (11/12) of IDPN-treated mice showed a decrease in aVOR and an increase in OKR.
source: The vast majority (n=11/12) of IDPN-treated mice showed a decrease in aVOR and an increase in OKR (top left quadrant corner, Figure 5B), which was not the case for SHAM mice (blue squares).
evidence: This is demonstrated by individual data plotted in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no correlation between the amplitude of VOR decrease and the amplitude of OKR increase.
source: However, there was no correlation between the amplitude of the VOR decrease and the amplitude of the OKR increase, that is mice that had the greatest VOR loss did not show the largest OKR increase (slope in the regression line: 0.27, p=0.0834).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At 0.2 Hz, there was a significant decrease in aVOR but the OKR was not modified.
source: At 0.2 Hz, there was a significant decrease in aVOR (IDPN W0 vs. W8 0.2 Hz p<10–4); however, the OKR was not modified.
evidence: This is supported by frequency-specific analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At 0.5 and 1 Hz, significant VOR decreases were accompanied by a significant OKR increase.
source: On the other hand, at 0.5 and 1 Hz significant VOR decreases (IDPN W0 vs. W8, 0.5 Hz, p<10–4; 1 Hz, p<10–4) were accompanied by a significant OKR increase (IDPN W0 vs. W8, 0.5 Hz, p<10–4; 1 Hz, p<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by frequency-specific analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At week 8, the change in OKR occurred at frequencies for which the vestibular weight is dominant (>50%).
source: Figure 5D shows that at week 8, the change in the OKR occurred at the frequencies for which the vestibular weight is dominant (>50%), and that the increase in OKR was positively correlated with the vestibular weight among frequencies (slope of the regression line: 1.235, r²=0.6299, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Model predictions for SHAM mice well-matched experimental CGR data.
source: as expected, model predictions for SHAM well-matched experimental data (Post-hoc Newman-keuls, SHAM MODEL vs SHAM CGR, p=0.41).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The model predicted that CGR gain of IDPN mice should be lower compared to SHAM.
source: When applied to IDPN mice the model predicted that their CGR gain should be lower compared to SHAM (shaded blue and red areas on Figure 6A and B, Post-hoc Newman-keuls, SHAM MODEL vs IDPN MODEL, p=0.00176)
evidence: This is supported by modeling results and statistical analysis shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: CGR gains observed for IDPN-treated mice were reduced compared to SHAM.
source: The CGR gains observed for IDPN-treated mice actually revealed how their visuo-vestibular responses were not only reduced compared to SHAM (compare solid blue and red lines in Figure 6A–B, Post-hoc Newman-keuls, SHAM CGR vs IDPN CGR, p=0.00055)
evidence: This is supported by experimental CGR data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: IDPN-treated mice CGR responses were inferior to the prediction of the model.
source: but were even inferior to the prediction of the model (compare solid red line and shaded red area in Figure 6B, Post-hoc Newman-keuls, IDPN MODEL vs IDPN CGR, p=0.00041).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of modeled and measured CGR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: IDPN-treated mice sub-optimally combined their residual/compensated vestibular and visual reflexes to stabilize gaze.
source: This suggests that the IDPN-treated mice sub-optimally combined their residual/compensated vestibular and visual reflexes to stabilize gaze.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that measured CGR was lower than predicted CGR in IDPN mice, as shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: There was a strong correlation between inter-sweep reproducibility and the capacity of mice to stabilize gaze in presence of vestibular inputs at light.
source: There was a strong correlation between the inter-sweep reproducibility and the capacity of the mice to stabilize gaze in presence of vestibular inputs at light.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The incapacity of the Δ- group to compute optokinetic signals in the presence of vestibular stimulation could relate to the poor reliability of the vestibular signal.
source: This result suggests that the incapacity of the Δ- group to compute optokinetic signals in the presence of vestibular stimulation could relate to the poor reliability of the vestibular signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between VOR reproducibility and CGR-OKR difference shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The presence of a degraded vestibular signal of significant amplitude but poorly reliable can be detrimental to properly stabilize gaze in presence of visual and vestibular inputs.
source: Overall, these data suggest that in some situations the presence of a degraded vestibular signal of significant amplitude (panel 6E) but poorly reliable (panel 6 F) can be detrimental to properly stabilize gaze in presence of visual and vestibular inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of VOR amplitude and reproducibility shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: IDPN has been established as an ototoxic compound targeting vestibular HC in different vestibular endorgans of rats.
source: IDPN has long been established as an ototoxic compound targeting vestibular HC in the different vestibular endorgans of rats (Llorens et al., 1993; Llorens et al., 1994b; Llorens and Demêmes, 1994a) and later in guinea-pig, frogs, and mice (Soler-Martín et al., 2007; Greguske et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on IDPN ototoxicity.

claim: The ototoxic effects of IDPN lead to early dismantlement of calyceal junction followed by synaptic uncoupling, both of which are reversible.
source: These previous studies further demonstrated some of the cellular mechanisms associated with the progressive loss of postural control: ototoxic effects lead to the early dismantlement of calyceal junction, followed by synaptic uncoupling, both of which were shown to be reversible
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on IDPN cellular mechanisms.

claim: Continuation of IDPN treatment leads to hair cell extrusion and long-term, permanent lesion.
source: while continuation of the IDPN treatment would lead to hair cell extrusion and long-term, permanent lesion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on IDPN effects.

claim: HC loss occurs in a central to peripheral order within vestibular epithelia, and in crista to utricule to saccule order.
source: HC loss was also demonstrated to occur in a central to peripheral order within vestibular epithelia, and in crista to utricule to saccule order (see Sedó-Cabezón et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sedó-Cabezón et al., 2015.

claim: Type I HC show greater sensitivity than type II HC to IDPN subchronic exposure.
source: Maroto et al., 2021 convincingly demonstrated that type I HC show greater sensitivity than type II HC to IDPN subchronic exposure.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maroto et al., 2021.

claim: Type I HC are crucial elements to encode both the amplitude and timing of the VOR, particularly for more dynamic stimulations.
source: These results could suggest that type I HC are crucial element to encode both the amplitude and timing of the VOR, particularly for the more dynamic stimulations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IDPN affects both gain and phase of VOR, with greater effects at higher frequencies, and correlates with type I HC loss.

claim: The vestibulo-ocular reflex can serve as a proxy indicating the status of the vestibular endorgans.
source: Overall, these organ-specific structure-function correlations confirm that the vestibulo-ocular reflex can serve as a proxy indicating the status of the vestibular endorgans.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlations between HC counts and VOR/OCR function shown in Figure 3.

claim: The use of aVOR and OCR as relevant tests reflects HC integrity at the level of ampullae and maculae, respectively.
source: It further validates the use of the aVOR and OCR as relevant tests reflecting HC integrity at the level of the ampullae and maculae, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the organ-specific correlations between HC counts and VOR/OCR function shown in Figure 3.

claim: The subchronic treatment affected type I HC more than type II HC.
source: The subchronic treatment affected type I HC more than type II HC, in accordance with previous reports (Llorens et al., 1993; Maroto et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Susceptibility to IDPN varies between different mouse strains.
source: Susceptibility to IDPN was also reported to vary between different mouse strains (Boadas-Vaello et al., 2017; Wilkerson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on strain differences.

claim: Loss of CASPR1 marker induced by IDPN sub-chronic treatment has been linked to HC detachment from the calyx terminal and loss of vestibulo-spinal reflexes.
source: The loss of CASPR1 marker induced by IDPN sub-chronic treatment has been linked to HC detachment from the calyx terminal and loss of vestibulo-spinal reflexes, and both CASPR1 expression and vestibular function recover during washout (Sedó-Cabezón et al., 2015; Greguske et al., 2019; Maroto et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on CASPR1 and IDPN effects.

claim: In adult rodents, regeneration of hair cells leads to formation of cells with type II HC features.
source: In adult rodents, however, the regeneration of hair cells leads to the formation of cells with type II HC features (González-Garrido et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to González-Garrido et al., 2021.

claim: Type I and type II HC differ by anatomical location, electrophysiological properties, morphology and innervation by afferents.
source: Type I and type II HC differ by many features, including their anatomical location within the epithelium, electrophysiological properties, morphology and innervation by afferents (Eatock and Songer, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eatock and Songer, 2011 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Irregular afferents predominantly innervate the central area and striolar zones with calyx and dimorphic synaptic contacts.
source: Seemingly, irregular afferents have been described as predominantly innervating the central area and striolar zones of the ampullae and maculae with calyx and dimorphic synaptic contacts
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldberg, 2000; Eatock and Songer, 2011; Contini et al., 2022.

claim: Regular afferents make dimorphic and button contacts predominantly within peripheral zones of cristae and extrastriolar zones of maculae.
source: while regular afferents make dimorphic and buttons contacts predominantly within the peripheral zones of cristae and extrastriolar zones of maculae (Goldberg, 2000; Eatock and Songer, 2011; Contini et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on vestibular afferent innervation patterns.

claim: Afferents with bouton terminals that contact only type II HC have regular discharge.
source: Afferents with bouton terminals that contact only type II HC have regular discharge
evidence: This represents established knowledge about vestibular afferent physiology.

claim: Afferents with calyx terminals that contact only type I HC have irregular discharge.
source: while afferents with calyx terminals that contact only type I HC have irregular discharge.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about vestibular afferent physiology.

claim: Most regular and irregular afferents are fed by both type I and type II HC.
source: However, most regular and irregular afferents are fed by both type I and type II HC (Goldberg et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldberg et al., 1992.

claim: Regular afferents recorded in the monkey show a lower detection threshold than irregular afferents.
source: Functionally, regular afferents recorded in the monkey show a lower detection threshold than irregular afferents (Sadeghi et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sadeghi et al., 2007.

claim: Irregular afferents show higher gains and phase leads and are better optimized for encoding high dynamic stimuli.
source: while irregular afferents showing higher gains and phase leads (mouse: Lasker et al., 2008; Cullen, 2019) would be better optimized for encoding high dynamic stimuli (Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lasker et al., 2008 and Cullen, 2019.

claim: Central VOR neurons receive a mixture of regular and irregular afferent inputs.
source: Central VOR neurons receive a mixture of regular and irregular afferent inputs (Goldberg et al., 1987; Boyle et al., 1992; Goldberg, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on central vestibular neuron inputs.

claim: Irregular afferents constitute approximately 1/3 of the excitatory drive to central VOR neurons.
source: with irregular afferents constituting ~1/3 of their excitatory drive (Goldberg et al., 1987; Boyle et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldberg et al., 1987 and Boyle et al., 1991.

claim: Functional ablation targeting irregular afferents suggested that VOR might function normally with only intermediate and regular afferent inputs.
source: Functional ablation targeting irregular afferents suggested that VOR might function normally with only intermediate and regular afferent inputs (Minor and Goldberg, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Minor and Goldberg, 1991.

claim: The most regular VOR neurons are particularly well-suited to faithfully encode compensatory eye movements generated during natural stimulation.
source: Functionally identified VOR neurons (i.e. PVP) were recently demonstrated to have heterogeneous discharge variability (high or low), with the most regular units particularly well-suited to faithfully encode the compensatory eye movements generated during natural stimulation (Mackrous et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mackrous et al., 2020.

claim: The two phasic/irregular and tonic/regular channels for head motion signals are constituted of both types I and type II HC.
source: However, the correspondence between hair cell properties and afferents/central neurons properties is only partial, such that the two phasic/irregular and tonic/regular channels for head motion signals are constituted of both types I and type II HC (Baird et al., 1988; Goldberg et al., 1990 p.90) and afferents (irregular and regular) (Goldberg, 2000; Eatock and Songer, 2011; Beraneck and Straka, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on vestibular signal processing.

claim: Carey et al., 1996 reported a better correlation of VOR recovery with type I than with type II HC following ototoxic lesions in the chick.
source: Carey et al., 1996 previously reported a better correlation of VOR recovery with type I than with type II HC following ototoxic lesions in the chick.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carey et al., 1996.

claim: Both type I and type II HC contribute to otolithic vestibular evoked potential responses.
source: It has also been recently shown that both type I and type II HC actually contribute to otolithic vestibular evoked potential responses (i.e. vestibulo-spinal pathway), previously described as mostly type I-specific (Sayyid et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sayyid et al., 2019.

claim: OKR plasticity following vestibular loss concerned gain, and not phase, modifications for frequencies >0.33 Hz.
source: OKR plasticity following vestibular loss concerned gain, and not phase, modifications for frequencies >0.33 Hz.
evidence: This is supported by the OKR data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: Previous studies have reported an increase in OKR gain following permanent vestibular lesion for a non-specific range of frequencies.
source: Previous studies have reported an increase in OKR gain following a permanent vestibular lesion for a non-specific range of frequencies (Shinder et al., 2005; Faulstich et al., 2006; Nelson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on OKR plasticity.

claim: Visual inputs could be reweighted and potentiated specifically in the range where vestibular loss has the most impact on gaze stabilization.
source: The visual inputs could be reweighted and potentiated specifically in the range where the vestibular loss has the most impact on gaze stabilization (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between OKR increase and vestibular weight shown in Figure 5D.

claim: VOR and OKR work synergistically to stabilize gaze by compensating for head and visual surround movements, respectively.
source: The VOR and OKR work synergistically to stabilize gaze by compensating for head and visual surround movements, respectively (França de Barros et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to França de Barros et al., 2020 and represents established knowledge.

claim: If reflexive eye movements are not perfectly compensatory, an error signal (retinal slip) is produced that drives adaptation of the VOR and OKR.
source: If the reflexive eye movements are not perfectly compensatory, an error signal (e.g retinal slip) is produced that drives adaptation of the VOR (Boyden et al., 2004; Dean and Porrill, 2014; Shin et al., 2014) and OKR (Glasauer, 2007; Kodama and du Lac, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on VOR and OKR adaptation mechanisms.

claim: Holland et al., 2020 proposed that OKR would account for the retinal slip not compensated by VOR.
source: In an effort to understand the integration of VOR and OKR (Holland et al., 2020) recently proposed that OKR would account for the retinal slip not compensated by VOR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holland et al., 2020.

claim: The integration of visual and vestibular signals during CGR is more than a mere summation of the gain and phase of the two unimodal reflexes.
source: This observation suggests that the integration of visual and vestibular signals during CGR is more than a mere summation of the gain and phase of the two unimodal reflexes, but is also affected by other factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that measured CGR differs from predicted CGR based on simple summation, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: According to statistical optimality theories, the decrease in VOR reliability should lead to a reduction in its relative sensory weight.
source: According to statistical optimality theories, as the Maximum Likelihood principle, the decrease in VOR reliability should lead to a reduction in its relative sensory weight.
evidence: This is based on established theories of multisensory integration.

claim: Filtering-out of a degraded signal has been shown during visuo-vestibular integration for monkey heading perception.
source: This filtering-out of a degraded signal has been shown during visuo-vestibular integration for monkey heading perception (Fetsch et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fetsch et al., 2010.

claim: Filtering-out of degraded signals has been shown for human object discrimination using visual and haptic senses.
source: or for human object discrimination using visual and haptic senses (Ernst and Banks, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ernst and Banks, 2002.

claim: The gaze stabilizing system is not able to optimally adapt to degradation by filtering-out vestibular signals during combined visuo-vestibular combination.
source: Our results suggest that the gaze stabilizing system is not able to optimally adapt to the degradation by filtering-out vestibular signals during combined visuo-vestibular combination.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some IDPN mice show worse CGR than OKR alone, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: The integration of visual and vestibular inputs occurs in several structures, including cerebellar flocculi and brainstem.
source: The integration of visual and vestibular inputs occurs in several structures, including in the cerebellar flocculi (Jang et al., 2020) and brainstem (Carcaud et al., 2017; see review De Zeeuw et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on visuo-vestibular integration sites.

claim: After unilateral neurectomy, vestibular neurons in the Deiters nuclei responded to higher frequencies during visual stimulation.
source: After unilateral neurectomy, vestibular neurons in the Deiters nuclei responded to higher frequencies during visual stimulation (Cat: Zennou-Azogui et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zennou-Azogui et al., 1994.

claim: Inhibitory floccular inputs and excitatory vestibular inputs often colocalize on the dendrites of central vestibular neurons.
source: It was shown that inhibitory floccular inputs (part of the OKR indirect pathway) and excitatory vestibular inputs often colocalized on the dendrites of central vestibular neurons.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about vestibular neuron anatomy.

claim: Massive disorganization of vestibular periphery inputs could lead to synaptic and intrinsic changes at the level of central vestibular neurons, impairing their capacity to optimally integrate both signals.
source: One possibility is therefore that the massive disorganization of vestibular periphery inputs led in the long term to synaptic and intrinsic changes at the level of central vestibular neurons (Beraneck and Idoux, 2012; Carcaud et al., 2017), thus impairing their capacity to optimally integrate both signals.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known plasticity mechanisms and the observed impairments in visuo-vestibular integration.

claim: Balance dysfunction occurs frequently in aging people with 85% prevalence above 80 years old.
source: Balance dysfunction occurs frequently in aging people (85% prevalence above 80; Agrawal et al., 2013) but also in younger people (prevalence of 35% in the 40-year-old).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agrawal et al., 2013.

claim: Many diseases consist of gradual, transient and/or partial loss of vestibular function rather than permanent vestibular lesions.
source: While animal models often use permanent vestibular lesions (Simon et al., 2020), many diseases in fact consist in a gradual, transient and/or partial loss of vestibular function.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2020 and clinical knowledge.

claim: Menière's disease represents approximately 9% of all vestibular pathologies in adults and occurs in those under 60 years old.
source: For instance Menière's disease, which represents ~9% of all vestibular pathologies in the adult and occurs in the <60 years old
evidence: This represents clinical knowledge about Menière's disease epidemiology.

claim: Menière's disease is characterized by recurrent episodes with brief (<24 hr) fluctuating symptoms and otherwise normal vestibular function before long-term deterioration arises.
source: is characterized by recurrent episodes with brief (<24 hr) fluctuating symptoms and otherwise normal vestibular function before long-term deterioration arises (Lopez-Escamez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lopez-Escamez et al., 2015.

claim: In vestibular neuritis, vestibular function can recuperate up to a year after the initial loss.
source: Transitory vestibular symptoms are also commonly reported in vestibular neuritis where, although symptoms tend to rapidly disappear due to vestibular compensation, vestibular function can recuperate up to a year after the initial loss (Welgampola et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Welgampola et al., 2019.

claim: Gradual and partial vestibular loss is encountered as a side-effect of some ototoxic anti-cancer treatments with approximately 40% prevalence in treated patients.
source: Gradual and partial vestibular loss is also encountered as a side-effect of some ototoxic anti-cancer treatments (prevalence in treated patients ~40%; cisplatin; Paken et al., 2016; Prayuenyong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paken et al., 2016 and Prayuenyong et al., 2018.

claim: The loss and partial recovery of VOR is correlated with the integrity of type I HC.
source: We show that the loss, and then the partial recovery of the VOR, is correlated with the integrity of the type I HC, demonstrating for the first time their essential role in the VOR, whether of canalar or otolithic origin.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sensory (visual) substitution would theoretically compensate for vestibular loss, but injured mice have suboptimal responses when combining visual and vestibular information.
source: We show that sensory (visual) substitution would theoretically compensate for vestibular loss, but that injured mice have suboptimal responses when combining visual and vestibular information.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling and CGR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Impairment in multisensory integration is linked to the loss of 'reliability' of the vestibular signal, degraded by ototoxicity.
source: Finally, we show that this impairment in multisensory integration would be linked to the loss of 'reliability' of the vestibular signal, degraded by ototoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by the reproducibility analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Transitory peripheral infractions have long term consequences.
source: Overall, these results suggest that transitory peripheral infraction have long term consequences
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that visuo-vestibular integration remains impaired even after VOR recovery.

claim: The capacity of central vestibular structures to cope with sensorineural loss might critically depend on the integrity of the neural elements involved.
source: and that the capacity of central vestibular structures to cope (vestibular compensation; Cullen et al., 2010; Beraneck and Idoux, 2012; Lacour et al., 2016) with the sensorineural loss might critically depend on the integrity of the neural elements involved.
evidence: This is inferred from the overall results and supported by citations to literature on vestibular compensation.
